item.title: 韓國新人流行當婚禮蟑螂？場地難找、價格黑箱，不踩點就踩雷！韓國年輕人乾脆不辦婚禮去買房？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:title: 韓國新人流行當婚禮蟑螂？場地難找、價格黑箱，不踩點就踩雷！韓國年輕人乾脆不辦婚禮去買房？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:author: TODAY 看世界
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gs2qyDvhOm8

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解韓國年輕準新人為何甘願自掏腰包當「婚禮蟑螂」，深入陌生人婚宴實地暗訪考察的奇特文化現象。
  • 剖析疫後韓國婚禮市場供需失衡、價格黑箱與不透明服務所帶來的社會與經濟壓力。
  • 探討當昂貴婚禮成為負擔時，韓國年輕世代轉向不辦婚禮買房或選擇公家場地的婚姻價值觀轉變。

摘要

準新人假扮賓客：韓國興起的婚禮「暗訪」文化

作者提到，韓國日前發生有陌生男女包了約五萬韓元禮金領取餐券進場用餐的事件，引發關注。這群人並非白吃白喝的婚禮蟑螂，而是特地前來實地考察的準新人。在韓國二三十歲的準新人圈子裡，這種「暗訪」極為盛行，他們自備基本禮金、穿著得體，在場內暗中考察動線順暢度、燈光音響、補菜速度以及宴客菜餚的口味，甚至在社群上記錄開箱評分，交換第一手情報，以避免日後在自己的婚禮上踩雷。

價格飆漲與資訊黑箱：準新人不得不臥底的原因

作者指出，準新人甘冒風險去暗訪的主因在於結婚成本暴增。受到通膨與疫情期間大量小型婚宴會館倒閉影響，場地供需嚴重失衡，婚宴費用創下新高。更棘手的是婚慶市場的價格黑箱，包含場地附加費與婚紗、攝影、妝髮等「結婚三寶」多數未標明細項單價；業者甚至規定簽約前不准試菜，且設有極高的低消人數門檻與當天簽約的促銷壓力，若事後解約還得面臨業者索取遠高於法規的高額違約金。

政府規範成效有限與年輕世代的無聲抗議

面對婚禮亂象，作者表示雖然韓國官方曾推動價格透明化法規與專法，但因缺乏實質開罰且排除小型工作室，市場短期內仍未改善。這導致許多韓國年輕人開始選擇不辦婚禮，將省下的預算轉用於買房或度蜜月；即便想辦婚禮，也大幅轉向預約便宜的公家場地。在傳統婚禮的高昂成本與層層套路下，當代韓國年輕人只能在精打細算中尋求新的出路。

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gs2qyDvhOm8

上個月，韓國一對新人剛辦完婚禮，發現有兩人在櫃檯包了5萬韓元，約台幣1100元的禮金後，就拿了兩張餐券進場吃飯了。你可能會想，這不就是婚禮蟑螂嗎？但一般人對婚禮蟑螂的印象，通常是不給禮金，混進去白吃白喝，甚至打包、拿喜餅！這兩人雖然包得少了，但好歹有給錢、也沒惹事，所以他們到底為什麼要特地花錢，參加陌生人的婚禮呢？

item.title: 韓國偶像出道年齡越來越低是為了賺更多錢？家長砸大錢幫孩子擠進選秀窄門，孩子的夢想竟變成大人的生意？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:title: 韓國偶像出道年齡越來越低是為了賺更多錢？家長砸大錢幫孩子擠進選秀窄門，孩子的夢想竟變成大人的生意？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:author: TODAY 看世界
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uqNXVxv9u7M

值得閱讀的理由

  • 剖析韓國K-pop偶像出道年齡日益幼態化的產業結構與商業獲利邏輯。
  • 了解「K-pop教父」李秀滿重新出發後，如何以低齡跨國女團再度掀起市場話題與熱議。
  • 深入探討星夢背後的高昂補習成本如何演變成階級競爭，以及年幼偶像所承受的身心健康代價。

摘要

李秀滿攜低齡女團強勢回歸市場

由被譽為「K-pop教父」的李秀滿所創立的A2O娛樂，推出全新女團A2O LIGHT，出道新曲迅速登上韓國音源榜冠軍。然而，引發外界高度關注的是該團平均年齡僅15歲，最小成員甚至只有13歲，國中生年紀的出道引發了大眾對當前偶像生態的廣泛討論。

出道年齡逐年下修背後的商業算盤

數據顯示韓國偶像的出道年齡正逐年下降，這背後的主要推動力來自經紀公司的獲利考量。由於培養練習生的沉沒成本極高，且近半數團體在出道未滿三年便宣告解散，使得公司傾向讓偶像提早出道，藉此拉長其在市場上的黃金吸金週期。

偶像補習班盛行與家庭財力的階級競爭

隨著全球化競爭加劇，經紀公司對語言與各項技能的要求日益嚴苛，導致選秀門檻提早降至十歲左右。這股趨勢催生了昂貴的偶像補習班文化，使練習生培育從單純的才華比拼，逐漸轉化為考驗家庭經濟實力與階級資源的昂貴賭博。

幼年成名的身心重擔與社會倫理隱憂

過早踏入演藝圈的低齡偶像，必須承受高壓訓練所帶來的生理與身心失調，同時還得面對缺乏隱私與網路惡意的衝擊。儘管官方訂有未成年保護法規，但日常練習難以落實監督，更引發了過度兒童性化以及過早剝奪青少年探索多元人生發展選擇權的道德爭議。

=============

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uqNXVxv9u7M

最近韓國演藝圈出現一支超級年輕的女團，才剛出道，第一首歌就在29小時內衝上韓國最大音樂串流平台Melon的排行榜冠軍，成績相當驚人。更驚人的是，這支女團總共9個人，平均年齡只有15歲，最小的3位成員，竟然只有13歲！如果在台灣，大概就是國一、國二的年紀。但真正引起話題的，還有她們背後的製作人，竟然是有「K-pop教父」之稱的李秀滿。74歲的教父，帶著一群13歲少女重出江湖，這是什麼組合？而且，現在的K-pop偶像，真的有必要這麼年輕嗎？

  • 了解「K-pop教父」李秀滿重新出發後，如何以低齡跨國女團再度掀起市場話題與熱議。
  • 深入探討星夢背後的高昂補習成本如何演變成階級競爭，以及年幼偶像所承受的身心健康代價。

摘要

李秀滿攜低齡女團強勢回歸市場

由被譽為「K-pop教父」的李秀滿所創立的A2O娛樂，推出全新女團A2O LIGHT，出道新曲迅速登上韓國音源榜冠軍。然而，引發外界高度關注的是該團平均年齡僅15歲，最小成員甚至只有13歲，國中生年紀的出道引發了大眾對當前偶像生態的廣泛討論。

出道年齡逐年下修背後的商業算盤

數據顯示韓國偶像的出道年齡正逐年下降，這背後的主要推動力來自經紀公司的獲利考量。由於培養練習生的沉沒成本極高，且近半數團體在出道未滿三年便宣告解散，使得公司傾向讓偶像提早出道，藉此拉長其在市場上的黃金吸金週期。

偶像補習班盛行與家庭財力的階級競爭

隨著全球化競爭加劇，經紀公司對語言與各項技能的要求日益嚴苛，導致選秀門檻提早降至十歲左右。這股趨勢催生了昂貴的偶像補習班文化，使練習生培育從單純的才華比拼，逐漸轉化為考驗家庭經濟實力與階級資源的昂貴賭博。

幼年成名的身心重擔與社會倫理隱憂

過早踏入演藝圈的低齡偶像，必須承受高壓訓練所帶來的生理與身心失調，同時還得面對缺乏隱私與網路惡意的衝擊。儘管官方訂有未成年保護法規，但日常練習難以落實監督，更引發了過度兒童性化以及過早剝奪青少年探索多元人生發展選擇權的道德爭議。

item.itunes:title: 強調素人參政、撇清黨派，第三勢力拚翻轉！美期中選舉掀「政黨切割潮」，選民最後卻含淚看黨投票？【TODAY 看世界】
item.itunes:author: TODAY 看世界
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcnsa_zv04U

值得閱讀的理由

  • 解析候選人為何刻意淡化政黨色彩，改以職業經歷與個人特質爭取選民認同。
  • 說明政黨不受歡迎、經濟焦慮與對政治老手的不滿，如何改變美國選戰策略。
  • 揭示「反建制」形象與實際投票行為之間的落差，並比較政黨標籤在不同選舉層級的影響。

摘要

從政黨色彩轉向個人品牌

選舉期間，候選人往往以政黨代表色彰顯政治立場，但作者指出，近年有些人開始改用個人風格建立品牌。以台北市長參選人沈伯洋為例，他的主要競選視覺採用橘色，搭配「讓台北流動」的口號，而不是以民進黨的綠色為主。這並非完全切斷政黨連結，而是呈現候選人不必只靠政黨認同，也能凸顯自身形象的趨勢。

政治素人與反建制形象

美國選戰也出現相似現象，而且更加鮮明。消防員、咖啡師、歌手、牧師、記者與運動教練等不同背景的參選者，常先介紹自己的職業與人生經歷，而非大聲宣示黨籍。部分候選人甚至以獨立身分參選，或在廣告中批評自己所屬政黨。作者指出，自2016年以來，進入國會的政治圈外人士比例明顯上升，政治新手因此成為候選人與政黨塑造新鮮感的重要資源。

淡化黨籍背後的政治盤算

候選人看似與政黨保持距離，卻不一定真的脫離政黨。部分自稱素人的參選者，仍獲得大量政黨資金支持；政黨也可能安排候選人退選，替特定人選鋪路。作者說明，兩大黨都在操作「不想當典型政客」的形象，因為選民對政黨愈來愈反感。民調顯示，不喜歡兩大黨的民眾比例升高，自認為獨立選民的人數也創下新高；在「負面黨派認同」盛行的環境裡，選民往往不是出於喜愛而支持某黨，而是為了阻止另一黨勝選。候選人淡化黨籍，便有機會讓對手陣營的選民暫時放下成見。

經濟焦慮與對老政治的厭倦

作者歸納出另外兩項原因。首先是生活成本與經濟壓力：物價上漲時，選民更在意油價與日常開支，執政黨候選人也更容易因政府施政受到責難。部分共和黨參選人因此與川普及黨內建制派拉開距離；民主黨候選人則試圖回應選民對政黨過度強調身分政治、忽略民生議題的不滿。其次，選民厭倦長期執政的老面孔，期待政治出現變化。以新職業、新世代候選人展現「換一批人試試看」，便成為爭取支持的策略。

選民喜歡反建制，投票時仍看政黨

不過，選民口頭上喜歡政治圈外人士，不代表投票時就會選擇第三黨或跨黨支持。調查顯示，雖然許多美國人不滿兩大黨，真正願意投給第三黨的人仍然很少。政治學實驗也發現，選民喜歡「我和華府那群人不一樣」的說法，但候選人是否真是政治素人，影響並沒有想像中大；選民更在意的是反建制的形象。然而，政黨認同依然強大：自2012年以來，多數州的參議員選舉結果都與該州最近一次總統大選的勝方一致，2016年甚至有34州在總統與參議員選舉中選出同一政黨。

地方選舉更看重候選人本身

候選人的個人形象並非毫無作用。研究發現，選舉層級愈地方化，選民愈可能跨越黨派界線；在南卡羅來納州，川普支持者於國會選舉分裂投票的比例只有5%，到了郡議會選舉升至23%，警長選舉則接近一半。這顯示地方選舉中，選民更重視候選人的經驗、辦事能力與親民程度；但在國會或總統大選裡，政黨標籤仍較有影響力。作者最後將這股風潮解讀為選民對現況失望、期待嘗試新選擇的表現，並邀請觀眾思考：投票時政黨有多重要，自己是否曾跨黨派投票，以及這種選擇是否會因地方與總統選舉而不同。

================================================

Whenever election season arrives, you see campaign billboards in all sorts of colors. In the past, candidates loved to plaster their party’s signature colors everywhere, fearing people wouldn't know their affiliation, but things are different now. For instance, Shen Po-yang, running for Taipei mayor this year for the DPP, avoided the party's signature green in his main campaign visuals, opting instead for a warm, sunny orange paired with the slogan "Make Taipei Flow." Shen explains that orange better represents his personal characteristics. While he didn't explicitly say this was to. downplay his green camp ties—since green elements still appear in other materials—it shows that candidates don't have to rely solely on party identity; they can build their own political brand. This recent US midterm election saw a similar trend, and they took it even further. A group of baristas and firefighters looking to serve the public are racing for Congress, each emphasizing they aren't career politicians; some are even dropping party affiliations entirely, or going so far as to criticize their own party in campaign ads. Isn't running for office usually about.

relying on the party's aura to attract votes? Why are these people desperately trying to act like they don't know their own parties? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Chi, and welcome to Fan Chi’s World View. It’s noted that many federal congressional candidates this year no longer lead their rallies by shouting their party; instead, they introduce themselves as pastors, journalists, or football coaches, hoping voters remember their personal traits rather than the party behind them. Most of those doing this are. political novices; studies show that while over 70%of newly elected US representatives used to be political veterans, since 2016, the share of political outsiders entering Congress has risen significantly, now accounting for half. In the Democratic House races , we’ve seen firefighters, baristas, and even a Latin singer who performed for nearly 30 years and opened up their microphone for the campaign. The Republicans are also playing the novice card, sending a TV sports reporter to run for senator; their support is even.

rivaling the incumbent Democratic lieutenant governor, aiming to snatch the seat. These candidates from vastly different backgrounds are all trying to use their personal professional experience to dilute their party labels and distinguish themselves from polished, traditional politicians. Beyond downplaying party colors, some opt out of party labels entirely, such as a mechanic running as an independent to challenge a wealthy incumbent Republican senator, pitting grassroots labor against a moneyed politician, along with former Green Berets and. former tank commanders running as independents. For conservative voters, this tough, patriotic image is often more persuasive than any party label and much easier to win over voters. Independent voters; interestingly, even veteran politicians have started following suit. A veteran Democratic congressman of 20 years is now emphasizing his roots as a fifth-generation lumberjack, and a sitting representative claims they once skipped a congressional vote to return.

home and fish for salmon, all to stress they are locals, not high-and-mighty politicians. But are these candidates who "don't act like politicians" truly unaffiliated with political parties? Some candidates campaign as pastors, never mentioning party ties on stage, yet they are backed by millions in Democratic funding. Democrats may even force their own candidates to drop out at the last minute to clear the path for these specific political outsiders. The Republican Party has similar tactics, with campaign committees spending money on ads for their own candidates that highlight their. willingness to defy their own party. Analysts note that while candidates used to court centrist voters by emphasizing their ability to work across the aisle, many this year are campaigning on "non-partisan" platforms , even turning their fire inward to criticize the establishment on both sides. Statistics show that during this year's election, the number of ads where Democratic candidates spent their own money to criticize the Democratic Party is unprecedented. Why......are.

these people starting to downplay their party labels? There may be several reasons. First, political parties have become a burden. A Pew Research Center survey in May found that 26%of respondents dislike both parties, higher than in previous years. Gallup polls show that 45%of voters identify as independents, a historic record. Another underlying reason is what political scientists call "negative partisanship." In plain terms, it means "voting against the other side." Voters support a party not because they love it, but because they fear the other. party winning even more. In polls released this month, more than 70%of voters in both parties shared this sentiment. In such a climate, a candidate wearing a party label will inevitably lose points in the opponent's territory. It is better to brand oneself as an "outsider" so that voters who usually hate your party might be willing to set aside their prejudices and listen to you. Second, voter economic anxiety. As prices continue to rise, voters care more about their own wallets, which is particularly disadvantageous for candidates of the ruling party. While Trump himself may be satisfied with.

imposing tariffs or challenging Iran, these international achievements are a burden for candidates who must face their constituents daily. Voters feel you are too busy posturing abroad to care whether they can afford gas at home. Some candidates have therefore distanced themselves from Trump and the Republican establishment, even openly opposing some of his policies. The Democratic Party is facing a different kind of grassroots anger. Some voters believe the party establishment overemphasizes identity politics, political correctness, and "woke" issues, while ignoring the most pressing bread-and-butter concerns of. ordinary people. For candidates hoping to win their races, emphasizing their relatability has become a way to distance themselves from the party's existing image. Third, voters are fed up with the old guard and want a fresh change. According to reports, seven Democratic members of the House of Representatives have already been ousted in their own party primaries this year, the most since 2000, with five of them past standard retirement age. Many voters feel these individuals have served for years without bringing change, so highlighting new faces from.

different professions is meant to show they can bring a new atmosphere and that it's time for a shake-up. But are voters really buying it? The answer is likely that they say they are, but they don't necessarily vote that way. A Gallup poll last year found that while a majority of Americans claim to dislike both parties, only 15%are actually willing to cast their vote for a third party. Experiments conducted by political scientists have also found a. similar discrepancy. They created a fictional candidate and crafted three different profiles—political veteran, political outsider, and anti-establishment—finding that voters love the "I’m not like those people in D.C." rhetoric, but whether they are truly an outsider matters much less. In other words, what voters are buying is an anti-establishment image. The two major parties have caught on to this and are operating behind the scenes, just ensuring their candidates don't look like typical politicians. However, no matter how hard a candidate works to build a personal image, when.

it comes time to actually vote, party influence remains significant. Pew Research Center found that since 2012, as many as 90%of winning Senate candidates in the U.S. have aligned with the party that won their state in the most recent presidential election. To put it plainly, if a state supports the Republican Party in a presidential election, the senator elected in that state will usually also be a Republican . 2016 was even more extreme; 34 states held both presidential and Senate elections, and all 34 states chose the. same party for both. By 2020, only four states produced different results. What does this mean? It means voters may like a candidate's personal qualities, but when the moment to vote arrives, party loyalty is still more influential , especially in a climate of intense political polarization; some people vote not because they like their own party, but because they loathe the other one. This desire to prevent the other side from winning makes it even harder for voters to cross party lines.

However, this doesn't mean the personal image that candidates work so hard to build is all for nothing. A study this year analyzed actual voter records and found that the more local the level, the more willing voters are to cross party lines. Take South Carolina for example: a group of Trump supporters had only a 5%chance of splitting their ticket in congressional elections, but this rose to 23%for county council races and nearly half for sheriff elections. The study suggests that in local elections, voters care more about whether a candidate has experience, can. get things done, and is in touch with the people; party affiliation is secondary. Conversely, when voting for members of Congress or the President, a packaged "political outsider" image may not be effective, and people still prioritize party labels. Experts believe this trend reflects voter disillusionment, as life doesn't seem to improve regardless of whether they vote blue or red; thus, "trying someone new" has become an opportunity for candidates to gain support and a campaign strategy for parties to exploit. Taiwan’s elections are next.

month, so I’d like to ask: when you vote, how important is the candidate’s party to you? Have you ever crossed party lines to vote? Or are you okay with it in local elections but not for the presidential race? Let me know in the comments. If you like this program, please share it with others. This recent US midterm election saw a similar trend, and they took it even further. A group of baristas and firefighters looking to serve the public are racing for Congress, each emphasizing they aren't career politicians; some are even dropping party affiliations entirely, or going so far as to criticize their own party in campaign ads. relying on the party's aura to attract votes? Why are these people desperately trying to act like they don't know their own parties? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Chi, and welcome to Fan Chi’s World View. The Republicans are also playing the novice card, sending a TV sports reporter to run for senator; their support is even.

rivaling the incumbent Democratic lieutenant governor, aiming to snatch the seat. These candidates from vastly different backgrounds are all trying to use their personal professional experience to dilute their party labels and distinguish themselves from polished, traditional politicians. Beyond downplaying party colors, some opt out of party labels entirely, such as a mechanic running as an independent to challenge a wealthy incumbent Republican senator, pitting grassroots labor against a moneyed politician, along with former Green Berets and. former tank commanders running as independents. For conservative voters, this tough, patriotic image is often more persuasive than any party label and much easier to win over voters. Independent voters; interestingly, even veteran politicians have started following suit. A veteran Democratic congressman of 20 years is now emphasizing his roots as a fifth-generation lumberjack, and a sitting representative claims they once skipped a congressional vote to return.

home and fish for salmon, all to stress they are locals, not high-and-mighty politicians. But are these candidates who "don't act like politicians" truly unaffiliated with political parties? Some candidates campaign as pastors, never mentioning party ties on stage, yet they are backed by millions in Democratic funding. Democrats may even force their own candidates to drop out at the last minute to clear the path for these specific political outsiders. The Republican Party has similar tactics, with campaign committees spending money on ads for their own candidates that highlight their. willingness to defy their own party. Analysts note that while candidates used to court centrist voters by emphasizing their ability to work across the aisle, many this year are campaigning on "non-partisan" platforms , even turning their fire inward to criticize the establishment on both sides. Statistics show that during this year's election, the number of ads where Democratic candidates spent their own money to criticize the Democratic Party is unprecedented. Why......are.

these people starting to downplay their party labels? There may be several reasons. First, political parties have become a burden. A Pew Research Center survey in May found that 26%of respondents dislike both parties, higher than in previous years. Gallup polls show that 45%of voters identify as independents, a historic record. Voters support a party not because they love it, but because they fear the other. party winning even more. In polls released this month, more than 70%of voters in both parties shared this sentiment. imposing tariffs or challenging Iran, these international achievements are a burden for candidates who must face their constituents daily. different professions is meant to show they can bring a new atmosphere and that it's time for a shake-up. But are voters really buying it?
